slides.title: Real-World Order of Operations
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the prerequisite and it carries the day's one habit. 2x² with x = 3 is 2(9), which is 18 — not (2 · 3)², which is 36. The parentheses around the substituted value are what keep the exponent attached to the x alone. A board that answers 36 will make the same mistake on every formula today.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
One habit, and it prevents most of the errors in this lesson. When a letter is replaced by a value, the value goes inside parentheses — then the exponent stays attached to what it was attached to, and a negative value keeps its sign. Work the kinetic-energy formula out loud: the square happens to the 10 alone, then the product, then the half.
OFF: 'Every substituted value goes into parentheses. That single habit prevents half of what goes wrong in this lesson.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Two problems, the same three numbers, the same words, and two different operations. Circling the numbers and boxing the key words gives exactly the same markings on both — which is why the state guide names that strategy as a misconception rather than a method. What decides is what is happening: in the first, four dollars happens six times; in the second, fifteen dollars happens four times.
OFF: 'There is no word that tells you which operation to use. Read what is happening, not which words are present.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Two rules that cost marks on the state test more often than any arithmetic does. Carry the exact value as far as you can and round once, at the end: a fence of six sides each √200 feet long is 84.85 feet, and a student who rounds the side to 14 first loses most of a foot. Then the unit: feet, dollars, joules. An answer with no unit is not an answer to a real-world question.
OFF: 'Round once, at the very end. Rounding in the middle moves the answer, and it moves it further every step you take afterwards.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A formula with a power in it.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask what the exponent is attached to before a single value is substituted — it is attached to the v, not to the m and not to the half.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Substitute in parentheses, square the speed, then multiply. A board with 81,000,000 squared the whole product, since ½(1,200)(15) is 9,000; a board with 18,000 read v² as 2v. The unit is joules and a board without it is not finished.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same formula, smaller numbers. 12² is 144 and half of 850 is 425. Catches 5,100 (the square forgotten) and 26,010,000 (the whole product squared).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A cost with a rate and a flat fee.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask which of the three prices depends on the size of the floor and which does not. That question — not a key word — is what puts the parentheses where they go.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: The two per-square-foot prices go inside the group that is multiplied by the area; the flat fee stays outside it. A board with 81(2.89 + 0.75 + 95) put the installation inside and charged it 81 times; a board with 9(3.64) + 95 used the side instead of the area.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: One rate and one flat fee this time. 6² is 36 and 36(4.25) is 153. Catches 36(4.25 + 13.48) — the flat fee charged per square foot — and 6(4.25) + 13.48.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: The state guide's own backyard task, reduced to its arithmetic. 200 is not a perfect square, so the root is carried exactly and rounded once at the end — which is why this board is tagged out of the radicand scan. A board with 84 rounded the side to 14 first and lost most of a foot; that is the point of the board, so name it rather than marking it.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and it is the exit evidence. Both problems contain 15, 4 and 6 and both contain 'plus' and 'each', so circling and boxing produce identical markings — and the two answers are 39 and 66. Full credit needs both totals and a sentence saying that what decides is which quantity is repeated, not which words appear. A student who writes only the two numbers has done the arithmetic and missed the item.
